cards.back:
Sounds good! / Deal!

Literally: That walks!

*— On se retrouve à 8h ? — Ça marche !*
— Meet at 8? — Sounds good!

💡 Everyday, friendly; fine with colleagues too. Use it to accept a plan: *On se voit à 8h ? — Ça marche !* Also means 'it works': *Ça marche pas* = it's not working.

No worries / It's no big deal.

Literally: It's not serious.

*Tu as oublié ? C'est pas grave.*
You forgot? No big deal.

💡 Neutral. Spoken French drops the *ne*: *ce n'est pas* → *c'est pas*. Classic reply to *Pardon !* or *Désolé(e)*. Polite written form: *Ce n'est pas grave*.

Meh.

*— Le film était bien ? — Bof.*
— Was the movie good? — Meh.

💡 Informal. Add a shrug. Peak Parisian indifference. Answers 'how was it?': *C'était bien ? — Bof.* Also before an adjective: *bof, pas terrible*.

I don't care.

*Tu choisis, je m'en fiche.*
You choose, I don't care.

💡 Casual; fine with friends, a bit blunt elsewhere. Conjugate the pronoun: *Il s'en fiche*, *On s'en fiche*. Add *de*: *Je m'en fiche de ton avis*. *Je m'en fous* = ruder (mildly vulgar). Polite: *Ça m'est égal*.

That's doing my head in.

Literally: That's making me drunk.

*Ce bruit, ça me saoule.*
This noise is getting on my nerves.

💡 Informal; very common with young people. Pronounced *sool*. Subject is the annoying thing: *Ce boulot me saoule*, *Tu me saoules !* (rude to someone's face). Neutral: *Ça m'agace*.

To not be bothered / to feel too lazy

Literally: To have the phlegm.

*J'ai la flemme de faire la vaisselle.*
I can't be bothered to do the dishes.

💡 Informal; one of the most-used slang phrases in France. Follow with *de* + infinitive: *J'ai la flemme de cuisiner*. Fine with friends and relaxed colleagues, not with your boss.

To feel down / blue

Literally: To have the cockroach.

*Depuis qu'il est parti, j'ai le cafard.*
Since he left, I've been feeling down.

💡 Neutral. Popularised in this sense by Baudelaire — now everyday. Conjugate *avoir*: *J'ai le cafard*, *Ça me donne le cafard* = it gets me down. *Un cafard* is also a cockroach.

To stand someone up

Literally: To put down a rabbit.

*Il m'a posé un lapin hier soir.*
He stood me up last night.

💡 Informal but widely used. Conjugate with an indirect pronoun: *Il m'a posé un lapin*, *Elle lui a posé un lapin*. Mostly in the passé composé. Neutral: *Il n'est pas venu au rendez-vous*.

To cost an arm and a leg

Literally: To cost the eyes of the head.

*Ce sac coûte les yeux de la tête.*
This bag costs an arm and a leg.

💡 Neutral; also *coûter un bras*. Subject is the thing: *Cette voiture coûte les yeux de la tête*, *Ça m'a coûté les yeux de la tête*.

To fall in love at first sight

Literally: To have the lightning strike.

*Quand je l'ai vue, j'ai eu le coup de foudre.*
When I saw her, it was love at first sight.

💡 Neutral, romantic. Use *pour*: *J'ai eu le coup de foudre pour lui* — also for places or objects: *pour cet appartement*. *La foudre* = lightning: love strikes like lightning.

To put in your two cents

Literally: To put one's grain of salt.

*Il faut toujours qu'il mette son grain de sel.*
He always has to put his two cents in.

💡 Neutral; usually mildly critical — of someone butting in uninvited. Conjugate *mettre* + possessive: *Il met toujours son grain de sel*, *Je vais mettre mon grain de sel*.

To have bigger fish to fry

Literally: To have other cats to whip.

*Désolé, j'ai d'autres chats à fouetter.*
Sorry, I've got bigger fish to fry.

💡 Neutral, humorous. Conjugate *avoir*: *J'ai d'autres chats à fouetter*. Often a polite brush-off: I've got more important things to deal with.

To faint / pass out

Literally: To fall in the apples.

*Il faisait si chaud qu'elle est tombée dans les pommes.*
It was so hot she fainted.

💡 Informal and very common, even with family or at work. Conjugate with *être*: *Elle est tombée dans les pommes*. Medical/neutral: *s'évanouir*.

cards.front: **Ce n'est pas la mer à boire.**
cards.back:
It's not that hard.

Literally: It's not the sea to drink.

*Allez, c'est pas la mer à boire !*
Come on, it's not that hard!

💡 Neutral, encouraging; always negative. Often shortened: *C'est pas la mer à boire !* Image: it's not like you have to drink the whole sea.

It's raining cats and dogs.

Literally: It's raining ropes.

*Prends un parapluie, il pleut des cordes.*
Take an umbrella, it's pouring.

💡 Neutral, everyday. Image: rain so heavy it falls like ropes. Same pattern: *Il pleut à verse*. Casual alternative: *Il flotte* (informal).

Let's get back to the point.

Literally: Let's return to our sheep.

*Bon, revenons à nos moutons.*
OK, back to the topic at hand.

💡 Neutral and humorous. From a 15th-century farce. Great in meetings to steer back on topic after a tangent. Only used in this fixed *nous* form.

To be full of energy

Literally: To have the peach / the fry.

*Ce matin, j'ai la pêche !*
I'm full of beans this morning!

💡 Informal and upbeat. Conjugate *avoir*: *J'ai la pêche aujourd'hui !*, *T'as la frite ?* Opposite: *Je n'ai pas la pêche* = I'm not feeling great.

To be daydreaming / miles away

Literally: To be in the moon.

*Tu m'écoutes ? Tu es dans la lune.*
Are you listening? You're miles away.

💡 Neutral. Conjugate *être*: *Désolé, j'étais dans la lune.* Gentle — fine to say about kids, colleagues or yourself. Similar: *être ailleurs*.

To tell lies / tall tales

Literally: To tell salads.

*Arrête de me raconter des salades !*
Stop telling me stories!

💡 Informal. Conjugate and add *à qqn*: *Il me raconte des salades*, *Arrête de raconter des salades !* Softer than calling someone a liar (*menteur*).

To be very lazy

Literally: To have a hair in the hand.

*Lui, il a un poil dans la main.*
That guy is bone idle.

💡 Informal and mocking — said about someone, rarely to their face. Conjugate *avoir*: *Il a un poil dans la main*. Memory hook: a hand so idle hair grows on the palm.

To bug someone / be a pain

Literally: To break someone's feet.

*Tu me casses les pieds !*
You're driving me mad!

💡 Informal. Use an indirect pronoun: *Tu me casses les pieds !*, *Il nous casse les pieds*. Noun: *un casse-pieds* = a pain. Vulgar version: *casser les couilles* — avoid. Neutral: *embêter*.

To sleep in

Literally: To do the fat morning.

*Dimanche, je fais la grasse mat'.*
On Sunday I sleep in.

💡 Neutral, everyday. Often shortened to *la grasse mat'*. Conjugate *faire*: *Dimanche, j'ai fait la grasse mat'*. Image: a 'fat' morning, packed with sleep.

To be dressed to the nines

Literally: To be pulled with four pins.

*Il est toujours tiré à quatre épingles.*
He's always impeccably dressed.

💡 Neutral, a bit elegant; can be slightly teasing. Conjugate *être* and agree: *Elle est tirée à quatre épingles*. Image: clothes pinned perfectly in place.

Easily / with my eyes closed

Literally: Fingers in the nose.

*J'ai réussi l'examen les doigts dans le nez.*
I passed the exam easily.

💡 Informal and fun; usually boastful. Adds to a verb: *J'ai eu mon permis les doigts dans le nez* = I passed my test easily. Neutral: *très facilement*.

When pigs fly

Literally: When hens have teeth.

*Il rangera sa chambre quand les poules auront des dents.*
He'll tidy his room when pigs fly.

💡 Neutral, humorous. Used to mock something that will never happen: *Il rangera sa chambre quand les poules auront des dents.* Note the future tense *auront*.

To be gutted / salty

Literally: To have the venom (from Arabic *sèmm*).

*On a perdu le match, j'ai le seum.*
We lost the match, I'm gutted.

💡 Youth slang, very current — friends only. Conjugate *avoir*: *J'ai le seum*, *Il a trop le seum*. Mix of anger and disappointment. Neutral: *Je suis dégoûté(e)*.

Weird / sketchy

Literally: Verlan (backwards slang) of *louche*.

*Ce type est chelou.*
That guy is sketchy.

💡 Informal verlan: syllables flipped, *louche* → *che-lou*. Invariable adjective: *un mec chelou*, *une ambiance chelou*. Friends only; neutral: *bizarre*.

That's crazy!

Literally: Verlan of *fou* (crazy).

*Ce concert était ouf !*
That concert was insane!

💡 Youth slang, friends only. Verlan of *fou*; also an adjective: *un truc de ouf* = something crazy. Neutral: *C'est fou !* / *C'est incroyable !*

To really like / love

Literally: From Arabic *kif* (pleasure).

*Je kiffe cette chanson.*
I love this song.

💡 Informal, friends only. Regular -er verb: *Je kiffe ce son*, *Il la kiffe* (he fancies her). Neutral: *adorer*, *aimer beaucoup*.

Totally / big time (intensifier)

Literally: Serious(ly).

*— Tu viens ? — Grave !*
— You coming? — Totally!

💡 Youth slang. As an intensifier: *J'ai grave faim*. Alone it means 'totally!': *T'es d'accord ? — Grave !* Friends only; neutral: *vraiment*, *carrément*.

So / as a result

Literally: Of the blow.

*Il pleuvait, du coup on est restés.*
It was raining, so we stayed in.

💡 Spoken, neutral; used constantly as a filler — like 'so' in English. Heard even at work, but avoid it in formal writing: use *donc* or *par conséquent*.

Anyway / long story short

Literally: Brief.

*Bref, on a raté le train.*
Anyway, we missed the train.

💡 Neutral; great conversation filler to cut a story short or wrap up: *Bref, on a raté le train.* Also a sighing 'anyway…' to change the subject.

Good luck! / Hang in there!

Literally: Good courage!

*Tu as un examen ? Bon courage !*
You've got an exam? Good luck!

💡 Neutral, works with anyone — boss, friend, stranger. Said for something difficult (exams, work, a move), not luck-based: for luck say *Bonne chance*. Reply: *Merci !*

Enjoy your meal!

Literally: Good appetite!

*Bon appétit à tous !*
Enjoy your meal everyone!

💡 Neutral; said before eating, and by waiters as they serve. Reply: *Merci, vous aussi !* / *Toi aussi !* Some very formal circles avoid it, but it's fine everywhere else.

Cheers!

Literally: Health! / To yours!

*À la vôtre !*
Cheers!

💡 *Santé !* works with anyone; *À la vôtre !* (formal/plural) or *À la tienne !* (one friend). Reply in kind: *À la vôtre !* Look people in the eyes when you clink glasses — tradition!

It's worth it.

Literally: It's worth the blow.

*Le musée ? Ça vaut le coup.*
The museum? It's worth it.

💡 Neutral. Negative: *Ça ne vaut pas le coup* = not worth it. Add *de* + infinitive: *Ça vaut le coup d'essayer*. Also *Ça vaut la peine*.

Nonsense! / Whatever!

Literally: No matter what!

*Il dit n'importe quoi.*
He's talking nonsense.

💡 Informal, very common. Reaction to nonsense: *N'importe quoi !* Also a building block: *n'importe qui* (anyone), *n'importe où* (anywhere). Can sound dismissive if aimed at someone.

Forget it / Never mind.

Literally: Let it fall.

*Laisse tomber, c'est pas important.*
Forget it, it's not important.

💡 Informal (*tu* form). Polite/plural: *Laissez tomber*. Means 'drop it': forget it, never mind, or give up on something. *J'ai laissé tomber le piano* = I gave up piano.

I'm sick of it.

Literally: I have had enough of it.

*J'en ai marre de ce temps !*
I'm sick of this weather!

💡 Informal, extremely common — fine with friends and relaxed colleagues. Add *de*: *J'en ai marre de ce temps*, *J'en ai marre d'attendre*. Stronger: *J'en ai ras le bol*.

How's it going?

Literally: Is it rolling?

*Salut ! Ça roule ?*
Hi! How's it going?

💡 Casual greeting, friends only. Reply: *Ça roule !* Also used alone to agree: *On se retrouve à 8h ? — Ça roule !* (like *Ça marche*).

Too bad / Oh well.

Literally: So much the worse.

*Il n'y a plus de pain ? Tant pis.*
No bread left? Oh well.

💡 Neutral; resigned acceptance. Also *tant pis pour toi/lui* = too bad for you/him (can sound harsh). Opposite: *Tant mieux* (so much the better).

Great! / So much the better!

Literally: So much the better.

*— J'ai eu le poste ! — Tant mieux !*
— I got the job! — Great!

💡 Neutral. Relieved or pleased reaction: *Il fait beau ? Tant mieux !* Also *tant mieux pour toi* = good for you. Opposite: *Tant pis*.

I can't believe it!

Literally: I'm not coming back from it.

*Tu as gagné ? J'en reviens pas !*
You won? I can't believe it!

💡 Neutral. Spoken: *J'en reviens pas*. Conjugate *revenir*: *Il n'en revenait pas* = he couldn't believe it. Add *de*: *Je n'en reviens pas de sa réponse*.

Don't mention it.

Literally: There's nothing for which.

*— Merci ! — Il n'y a pas de quoi.*
— Thanks! — Don't mention it.

💡 Neutral reply to *merci*. Spoken: *Y'a pas de quoi* or just *De rien*. More polite: *Je vous en prie*.

By the way…

*Au fait, tu as vu Marc ?*
By the way, have you seen Marc?

💡 Neutral. Pronounce the t: *oh fet*. Introduces a new topic: *Au fait, tu as vu Paul ?* Don't confuse with *en fait* (actually).

It's all the same to me.

Literally: It is equal to me.

*Pizza ou sushi, ça m'est égal.*
Pizza or sushi, I don't mind.

💡 Neutral and polite — safe at work. Polite version of *je m'en fiche*. Change the pronoun: *Ça lui est égal*. Can sound indifferent, so add *comme tu veux* to sound warmer.

We'll see.

Literally: One will see.

*— On part en vacances ? — On verra.*
— Shall we go on holiday? — We'll see.

💡 Neutral. A soft way to avoid committing — like English 'we'll see'. *On* = 'we' in spoken French. Also *Qui vivra verra* (time will tell).

It depends.

*Ça dépend du temps.*
It depends on the weather.

💡 Neutral. Add *de*: *Ça dépend du temps*, *Ça dépend de toi*. Natural follow-up question: *Ça dépend de quoi ?*

It's bliss! / It's the best!

Literally: It's the foot!

*Une semaine à la plage, c'est le pied !*
A week at the beach — it's the best!

💡 Informal, positive. *C'est pas le pied* = it's not great. Related: *prendre son pied* (careful, can be sexual).

I don't feel like it / doesn't ring a bell.

Literally: That says nothing to me.

*Ce nom ne me dit rien.*
That name doesn't ring a bell.

💡 Neutral, polite — two meanings depending on context: *Ça te dit d'aller au ciné ? — Ça ne me dit rien* (not keen); *Ce nom ne me dit rien* (doesn't ring a bell). Positive: *Ça me dit quelque chose*.

To be in the know / aware

Literally: To be in the current.

*Tu es au courant de la nouvelle ?*
Have you heard the news?

💡 Neutral, fine at work. Add *de*: *Tu es au courant de la réunion ?* Useful: *Je ne suis pas au courant* = I didn't know. *Je te tiens au courant* = I'll keep you posted.

I'll keep you posted.

Literally: I hold you in the current.

*Je te tiens au courant pour samedi.*
I'll let you know about Saturday.

💡 Neutral, very useful — friends and work. Polite/plural: *Je vous tiens au courant*. Ask for it: *Tiens-moi au courant !*

To have a lot on your plate

Literally: To have bread on the board.

*Cette semaine, j'ai du pain sur la planche.*
I've got a lot on my plate this week.

💡 Neutral, fine at work. Conjugate *avoir*: *On a du pain sur la planche*. Image: a board loaded with bread to slice — lots of work ahead.

To call a spade a spade

Literally: To call a cat a cat.

*Appelons un chat un chat : c'est un échec.*
Let's call it what it is: it's a failure.

💡 Neutral. Means speaking frankly without euphemisms — often as a justification: *Moi, j'appelle un chat un chat.*

To have a great time

Literally: To take one's foot.

*On a pris notre pied au concert.*
We had a blast at the concert.

💡 Informal. Careful: it can also mean to climax (sexual), so context matters. Safer: *s'éclater* (informal) or *bien s'amuser*. *J'ai pris mon pied au concert*.

To feel under the weather / off

Literally: To not be in one's plate.

*Je ne suis pas dans mon assiette aujourd'hui.*
I'm feeling a bit off today.

💡 Neutral, fine at work; usually negative. Conjugate + possessive: *Je ne suis pas dans mon assiette*, *Elle n'est pas dans son assiette*. Physically or emotionally off.

To sulk

Literally: To make the head.

*Pourquoi tu fais la tête ?*
Why are you sulking?

💡 Neutral. Conjugate *faire*: *Il fait la tête depuis ce matin*. Ask: *Tu fais la tête ?* = Are you sulking? Don't confuse with *faire la fête* (to party).

It's obvious.

Literally: It jumps to the eyes.

*Il est amoureux, ça saute aux yeux.*
He's in love, it's obvious.

💡 Neutral. Add *que* to state what's obvious: *Ça saute aux yeux qu'il est amoureux.* Also *Ça crève les yeux* (informal, stronger).

cards.front: **Petit à petit, l'oiseau fait son nid.**
cards.back:
Little by little, you get there.

Literally: Little by little, the bird makes its nest.

*Ne lâche pas le français : petit à petit, l'oiseau fait son nid.*
Don't give up on French: little by little, you'll get there.

💡 Proverb, neutral — encouraging. Your motto for learning French! Shorter: *petit à petit* = little by little.

Where there's a will, there's a way.

Literally: To want is to be able.

*Tu vas y arriver. Vouloir, c'est pouvoir.*
You'll get there. Where there's a will…

💡 Proverb, neutral — motivational. Same structure as English 'to want is to be able'.

Don't judge a book by its cover.

Literally: The habit doesn't make the monk.

*Il a l'air sévère, mais l'habit ne fait pas le moine.*
He looks stern, but don't judge a book by its cover.

💡 Proverb, neutral. Literally the habit (robe) doesn't make the monk: looks can deceive, especially about status or character.

Joy of living; zest for life

Literally: Joy of living.

*Elle a une vraie joie de vivre.*
She has a real zest for life.

💡 Neutral, a bit literary. Borrowed into English too. Used about a person or place: *Elle respire la joie de vivre* = she radiates zest for life.

Thinking of the perfect comeback too late

Literally: The wit of the staircase.

*J'ai trouvé la réplique parfaite… dans l'escalier.*
I found the perfect reply… on the way out.

💡 Coined by Diderot; a bit literary. English borrowed it too. Usually *avoir l'esprit de l'escalier*. Image: the comeback hits you on the way down the stairs.

To have the knack

Literally: To have the hand stroke.

*Faire des crêpes ? Il faut avoir le coup de main.*
Making crêpes? You need the knack.

💡 Neutral. Conjugate *avoir*: *Tu as le coup de main !* Learn it: *prendre le coup de main* = to get the hang of it. Don't confuse with *donner un coup de main* = to lend a hand.

To grab a drink

Literally: To drink a blow / a glass.

*On va boire un coup après le travail ?*
Shall we grab a drink after work?

💡 Informal and friendly; *un verre* is slightly more neutral. Invite: *On va boire un coup ?* / *Tu veux boire un verre ?* Implies alcohol unless specified.

It shows.

Literally: That sees itself.

*Tu es fatigué, ça se voit.*
You're tired, it shows.

💡 Neutral. Also *ça se voit que…*: *Ça se voit que tu es fatigué*. Negative: *Ça ne se voit pas* = you can't tell.

Are you out of your mind?

Literally: Is the head not OK?

*Sauter du pont ? Ça va pas la tête ?*
Jump off the bridge? Are you crazy?

💡 Informal, playful — friends only; can sound rude to a stranger. Full form: *Ça va pas, la tête ?* Neutral: *Tu es fou/folle ?*

Oh dear! / Wow! / Oh no!

*Oh là là, il est déjà midi !*
Oh my, it's already noon!

💡 Neutral, works anywhere. Never 'ooh la la' in a flirty way — French people use it for surprise or dismay. More *là*s = more emotion: *Oh là là là là !*

cards.front: **Il ne faut pas pousser mémé dans les orties.**
cards.back:
Don't push your luck / Don't go too far.

Literally: Don't push granny into the nettles.

*Un deuxième dessert ? Faut pas pousser mémé dans les orties !*
A second dessert? Don't push it!

💡 Humorous, informal. Often shortened: *Faut pas pousser mémé dans les orties !* Or even just *Faut pas pousser !* Image: pushing granny into the nettles is going too far.

To be out of it / spaced out

Literally: To be in the west.

*Désolé, je suis complètement à l'ouest ce matin.*
Sorry, I'm totally out of it this morning.

💡 Informal. Conjugate *être*: *Désolé, je suis complètement à l'ouest.* Stronger than *dans la lune* — confused, scatterbrained, or jet-lagged.

To have a hangover

Literally: To have a wooden mouth.

*Après la fête, j'avais la gueule de bois.*
After the party I had a hangover.

💡 Informal but used by everyone. Conjugate *avoir*: *J'ai la gueule de bois*. *Gueule* is slangy (mouth), so at work just say *Je suis fatigué(e)*.

To put your foot in it

Literally: To put your feet in the dish.

*Il a mis les pieds dans le plat en parlant de son ex.*
He put his foot in it mentioning her ex.

💡 Neutral. Conjugate *mettre*: *J'ai mis les pieds dans le plat*. Can also mean to raise a delicate topic bluntly on purpose. Image: stepping in the serving dish.

It's none of my business.

Literally: They're not my onions.

*Ça, c'est pas mes oignons.*
That's none of my business.

💡 Informal. *Occupe-toi de tes oignons* = mind your own business (rude). Change the possessive: *C'est pas tes oignons !* Neutral: *Ça ne me regarde pas*.

Don't worry about it!

Literally: (Don't) worry yourself!

*— Merci pour le coup de main ! — T'inquiète !*
— Thanks for the help! — No worries!

💡 Informal, friends only; short for *Ne t'inquiète pas*. Also used as 'you're welcome' or 'no problem'. Polite: *Ne vous inquiétez pas*.

No problem!

Literally: No worry!

*— Tu peux m'envoyer le fichier ? — Pas de souci !*
— Can you send me the file? — No problem!

💡 Neutral, everywhere — shops, emails, friends. Also *Y a pas de souci*. Common reply to *merci* or to a request. Purists prefer *pas de problème*, but this is universal.

Go ahead! / Go on!

Literally: Go there!

*— Je peux te poser une question ? — Vas-y !*
— Can I ask you something? — Go ahead!

💡 Informal (*tu*); polite/plural: *Allez-y !* Use it to let someone go first, start, or speak. Also cheering: *Vas-y, vas-y !* = Come on!

Coming! / I'll be right there!

Literally: I'm arriving!

*— À table ! — J'arrive !*
— Dinner's ready! — Coming!

💡 Neutral. Said even when you haven't moved yet. Reply when someone calls you. Also 'I'm managing': *Je n'arrive pas à…* = I can't manage to…

That's it! / Done! / Finally!

Literally: That's there!

*Ça y est, j'ai fini mon mémoire !*
That's it, I've finished my thesis!

💡 Neutral. *Ça y est ?* = Are you done? / Is it ready? *Ça y est, j'ai fini !* Signals the long-awaited moment has come.

Come on! / Right then! / Bye!

Literally: Go! (plural)

*Allez, on y va ! … Allez, salut !*
Come on, let's go! … Right, bye!

💡 Neutral. Used to encourage, to wrap up, or to say goodbye (*Allez, salut !*). Same form for *tu* and *vous*. Also football chant: *Allez les Bleus !*

Here we go! / Let's go!

Literally: It's off!

*Tout le monde est prêt ? C'est parti !*
Everyone ready? Here we go!

💡 Neutral, enthusiastic — fine anywhere. Said as you start something: *Tout le monde est prêt ? C'est parti !*

Shall we go?

Literally: We go there?

*Il est 8h, on y va ?*
It's 8, shall we go?

💡 Neutral. *Allez, on y va !* = Let's go! Spoken *on* = 'we'. Also *Vas-y* (to one person) vs *On y va* (us together).

Fancy it? / How does that sound?

Literally: Does that say (something) to you?

*On se fait un ciné ce soir, ça te dit ?*
Movie tonight — are you up for it?

💡 Informal. *Ça vous dit ?* for several people or politely. Add *de* + infinitive: *Ça te dit d'aller au ciné ?* Reply: *Carrément !* or *Ça me dit bien*.

I'm in! / Count me in.

Literally: I'm leaving (= ready to go).

*— Un resto ce soir ? — Je suis partant !*
— Restaurant tonight? — I'm in!

💡 Informal but fine with colleagues. Agree the ending: *partant* (m) / *partante* (f). Add *pour*: *Je suis partant pour un resto*. Opposite: *Je ne suis pas très partant* = I'm not keen.

That works for me.

Literally: That goes to me.

*— Samedi à 14h ? — Ça me va.*
— Saturday at 2? — Works for me.

💡 Neutral, safe anywhere. Change the pronoun: *Ça vous va ?* = Does that suit you? Also for clothes: *Cette robe te va bien*.

That's good timing! / How convenient!

Literally: That falls well!

*Tu vas à la poste ? Ça tombe bien, j'ai une lettre.*
You're going to the post office? Good timing, I've got a letter.

💡 Neutral. Opposite: *Ça tombe mal* = bad timing. Often followed by a reason: *Ça tombe bien, j'allais t'appeler !*

You said it! / Too right!

Literally: It's clear!

*— Ce prof est trop strict. — C'est clair !*
— That teacher's way too strict. — Totally!

💡 Informal agreement among friends. Can also mean 'that's obvious'. Neutral: *Tout à fait !*

Absolutely! / Definitely!

Literally: Squarely!

*— Tu viens à la fête ? — Carrément !*
— Coming to the party? — Absolutely!

💡 Informal. Also *carrément* + adj. = downright: *c'est carrément nul*. Enthusiastic reply to suggestions: *Ça te dit ? — Carrément !* Neutral: *Absolument*.

No wonder! / Tell me about it!

Literally: You astonish me!

*— Il est crevé, il a bossé toute la nuit. — Tu m'étonnes !*
— He's exhausted, he worked all night. — No wonder!

💡 Informal, ironic: means the opposite — 'that's not surprising at all'. *Il est fatigué ? Tu m'étonnes, il a dormi 3 heures !* Friends only.

No kidding?

Literally: Without joke?

*— Elle s'est mariée. — Sans blague ?*
— She got married. — No kidding?

💡 Informal. Can be sincere or sarcastic depending on tone. *Sans blague !* (falling tone) = No kidding, obviously!

You're joking!

Literally: Are you laughing?

*Cent euros pour ça ? Tu rigoles ?*
A hundred euros for that? Are you kidding?

💡 Informal. Also *Tu plaisantes ?* (neutral). Polite: *Vous plaisantez ?* Alone or as reaction to bad news: *Tu rigoles, c'est 50 euros ?*

For real?

Literally: Serious?

*— J'ai eu le job ! — Sérieux ? Bravo !*
— I got the job! — Seriously? Well done!

💡 Informal; short for *T'es sérieux ?* (*sérieuse* for a woman). Rising tone = disbelief. Neutral: *Vraiment ?*

Oh really? / Is that so?

Literally: Ah good?

*— Le magasin est fermé le lundi. — Ah bon ?*
— The shop's closed on Mondays. — Really?

💡 Neutral. The go-to reaction to new information. Rising tone = surprise; flat *Ah bon.* = mild acceptance. Safe with anyone.

I see.

*— Je suis un peu débordé. — Je vois.*
— I'm a bit swamped. — I see.

💡 Neutral. Can sound knowing or slightly skeptical, depending on tone. Also *Je vois ce que tu veux dire* = I see what you mean.

There you go! / Exactly! / That's it.

Literally: See there!

*— Donc il faut tourner à gauche ? — Voilà !*
— So I turn left? — Exactly!

💡 Neutral. French people end explanations with *voilà* constantly. Also when handing something over: *Voilà votre café*. *Et voilà !* = and there you have it.

Still! / Come on! / Really!

*Il aurait pu prévenir, quand même !*
He could have let us know, honestly!

💡 Neutral. Expresses mild indignation or 'all the same': *Il aurait pu appeler, quand même !* Also concessive: *Il pleut, mais on sort quand même*.

Honestly… / Frankly…

*Franchement, c'était le meilleur repas de l'année.*
Honestly, that was the best meal of the year.

💡 Neutral; used as a filler and for emphasis. Often starts an opinion: *Franchement, c'était nul.* Can sound like a mild reproach: *Franchement !* = Honestly!

Like… / As if…

Literally: Kind.

*Il m'a regardé genre j'existais pas.*
He looked at me like I didn't exist.

💡 Informal filler, like English 'like' — friends only, and avoid overusing. *Genre !* alone = 'As if!' Also *du genre* = sort of.

Basically / Roughly

Literally: In big.

*En gros, on doit tout refaire.*
Basically, we have to redo everything.

💡 Neutral; ubiquitous when summing up, even at work. Usually opens a summary: *En gros, il faut tout refaire.* Don't confuse with *en gros* = wholesale (commerce).

Not bad! / Pretty good!

Literally: Not badly!

*— J'ai eu 16 sur 20. — Pas mal !*
— I got 16 out of 20. — Not bad!

💡 Neutral understatement — often means 'really good'. Also quantity: *pas mal de gens* = quite a lot of people.

That's rubbish! / That's lame!

Literally: It's null!

*Ce film était nul.*
That movie was terrible.

💡 Informal. *T'es nul !* = You're useless! (hurtful if serious). Also *nul en maths* = rubbish at maths. Softer: *C'est pas terrible*.

That sucks! / That's dodgy.

Literally: It fears!

*Le train est annulé ? Ça craint !*
The train's cancelled? That sucks!

💡 Informal. Also 'dodgy': *Ce quartier craint*. Neutral: *C'est dommage* (shame) or *C'est embêtant*. Avoid in formal settings.

That's tough / tricky.

Literally: It's hot.

*Finir ça pour demain, c'est chaud.*
Finishing that by tomorrow is going to be tough.

💡 Informal, youth. *C'est chaud* = tricky or intense. But *Je suis chaud !* = I'm up for it! Neutral: *C'est difficile*.

It's going to be OK.

Literally: It's going to go.

*Respire, ça va aller.*
Breathe, it's going to be OK.

💡 Neutral, comforting — works with anyone. Ask how someone is coping: *Ça va aller ?* Reply: *Oui, ça va aller, merci.*

There's no need / No point.

Literally: It's not the trouble.

*C'est pas la peine de crier, j'entends.*
No need to shout, I can hear you.

💡 Spoken (*ne* dropped). Formal: *Ce n'est pas la peine*. Add *de* + infinitive: *C'est pas la peine de crier*. Also politely refusing help: *Non, c'est pas la peine*.

cards.front: **Je t'en prie / Je vous en prie.**
cards.back:
You're welcome (polite) / After you.

Literally: I pray you of it.

*— Merci ! — Je vous en prie.*
— Thank you! — You're welcome.

💡 Polite; *vous* form is more formal — perfect for strangers, shops, work. Also used to let someone go first or grant permission: *Je peux ? — Je vous en prie.*

With pleasure! / Gladly!

Literally: With pleasure!

*— Tu veux un café ? — Avec plaisir !*
— Want a coffee? — I'd love one!

💡 Neutral, warm. Also a reply to *merci* and an enthusiastic yes to an invitation: *Un café ? — Avec plaisir !* Safe with anyone.

I'm glad / It's my pleasure.

Literally: That makes me pleasure.

*Merci d'être venu, ça me fait vraiment plaisir.*
Thanks for coming, I'm really glad.

💡 Neutral. *Ça me ferait plaisir* = I'd love that. Also the gift giver's reply to thanks. Change pronoun: *Ça lui fera plaisir* = he/she'll be pleased.

See you later!

Literally: At more! / At all at the hour!

*Bon, j'y vais. À plus !*
Right, I'm off. See you!

💡 *À plus* (texts: *A+*) is informal; *à tout à l'heure* = later today. Slangy: *à toute !* Neutral for another day: *À bientôt*.

As usual

*— Il est en retard ? — Comme d'hab !*
— Is he late? — As usual!

💡 Informal, short for *comme d'habitude* (use that at work). Sounds like *comme dab*. *Comme d'hab, il est en retard.*

Long time no see!

Literally: That makes a lease!

*Salut ! Ça fait un bail !*
Hi! It's been ages!

💡 Informal, friends; *un bail* = a lease, i.e. a long time. Also *Ça fait un bail que je l'ai pas vu*. Neutral: *Ça fait longtemps !*

Worst case… / If all else fails…

Literally: At the worst.

*Au pire, on prend un taxi.*
Worst case, we'll take a taxi.

💡 Neutral, very common for proposing a backup plan: *Au pire, on prend un taxi.* Opposite: *Au mieux* = at best.

Still… / All the same…

Literally: (That) doesn't prevent…

*N'empêche, il avait raison.*
Still, he was right.

💡 Informal; concedes a point but still objects. Also *N'empêche que…*: *N'empêche qu'il avait raison.* Neutral: *Quand même* / *Tout de même*.

How do we do this? / What's the plan?

Literally: We do how?

*Il n'y a plus de place. On fait comment ?*
There's no room left. What do we do?

💡 Informal (spoken word order). Neutral: *Comment est-ce qu'on fait ?* Formal: *Comment fait-on ?*

It's worth a shot!

Literally: That tries itself!

*Un concert gratuit ? Ça se tente !*
A free concert? Worth a shot!

💡 Informal, upbeat. Encourages trying something uncertain: *Un nouveau resto ? Ça se tente !* Neutral: *Ça vaut le coup d'essayer*.

There's no comparison / No contest.

Literally: There's no photo (finish).

*Entre les deux, y a pas photo : je prends le premier.*
Between the two, there's no contest: I'll take the first.

💡 Informal; from horse racing's photo finish. Spoken: *Y a pas photo*. Use when one option clearly wins: *Entre les deux, y a pas photo.*

Without seeming to / Believe it or not

Literally: Look of nothing.

*Mine de rien, on a fait 20 km aujourd'hui.*
Believe it or not, we did 20 km today.

💡 Informal, very common. Usually at the start or middle: *Mine de rien, il a beaucoup progressé* = without making a fuss / you wouldn't think it, but.

It'll work out / It'll do.

Literally: That's going to do it.

*Une heure pour cuisiner ? Ça va le faire.*
An hour to cook? That'll be fine.

💡 Informal, reassuring — friends and relaxed colleagues. Neutral: *Ça va marcher* or *Ça ira*.

I doubt it.

Literally: That would astonish me.

*— Il va venir ? — Ça m'étonnerait.*
— Will he come? — I doubt it.

💡 Neutral, polite skepticism — safe at work. Add *que* + subjunctive: *Ça m'étonnerait qu'il vienne.*

That bodes well! / This should be good (ironic).

Literally: That promises!

*Il pleut déjà et on n'est pas partis… ça promet !*
It's raining already and we haven't even left… off to a great start!

💡 Neutral; often ironic: *Il pleut déjà ? Ça promet pour le week-end…* Tone tells you which meaning.

If you say so…

Literally: If you say it…

*— Je n'ai mangé qu'un seul cookie. — Si tu le dis…*
— I only ate one cookie. — If you say so…

💡 Neutral, skeptical — mildly cheeky. Polite/plural: *Si vous le dites…* Like English 'if you say so'.

I swear!

Literally: I swear to you!

*Je te jure, c'est vrai !*
I swear, it's true!

💡 Informal; youth often say *Wallah* or *J'te jure*. Also exasperation: *Je te jure, il est impossible !* Polite: *Je vous assure*.

While I think of it…

Literally: As long as I think of it.

*Tant que j'y pense, tu me dois dix euros.*
While I think of it, you owe me ten euros.

💡 Neutral, fine at work. Introduces something you might forget: *Tant que j'y pense, tu me dois 10 euros.*

A guy / A girl (woman)

*Ce mec, c'est le frère de ma meuf.*
That guy is my girlfriend's brother.

💡 Informal. *Meuf* is verlan of *femme*; *ma meuf* = my girlfriend, *mon mec* = my boyfriend. *Meuf* can sound disrespectful; neutral: *un homme / une femme*, *un gars*.

A buddy / mate

*Je sors avec des potes ce soir.*
I'm going out with some mates tonight.

💡 Informal, extremely common. Feminine: *une pote*. *C'est un pote à moi* = he's a mate of mine. Neutral: *un ami / une amie*.

Work / Job

*Je suis encore au boulot.*
I'm still at work.

💡 Informal, used by everyone; synonym *le taf*. *Je vais au boulot*, *Bon boulot !* = good job. Neutral: *le travail*.

To work

*Je bosse demain matin.*
I'm working tomorrow morning.

💡 Informal; *bosser pour un exam* = to study for an exam. Regular -er verb: *Je bosse demain*. Fine with colleagues. Neutral: *travailler*.

To be exhausted

Literally: To be burst / punctured.

*Je suis crevé, je vais me coucher.*
I'm beat, I'm going to bed.

💡 Informal. Agree: *Je suis crevée* (f). Also *être claqué*, *être naze*. Neutral: *Je suis épuisé(e)* / *très fatigué(e)*.

A thing / thingy

*C'est quoi, ce truc ?*
What's this thing?

💡 Informal, everywhere — use when you forget a word. *C'est pas mon truc* = it's not my thing. Also *un truc de fou* = something crazy. Neutral: *une chose*.

To eat / Food (grub)

*La bouffe était top, on a super bien bouffé !*
The food was great, we ate really well!

💡 Informal. Don't use with your in-laws on day one. Neutral: *manger* / *la nourriture*. *On bouffe où ?* = Where are we eating?

Money / Cash

*J'ai plus de thune.*
I'm out of cash.

💡 Informal; also *le fric*, *le blé*. *J'ai plus de thune* = I'm broke. Neutral: *l'argent*. Also spelled *tune*.

Annoying / A pain

Literally: Verlan of *lourd* (heavy).

*Il est relou avec ses questions.*
He's so annoying with his questions.

💡 Informal verlan of *lourd*, very common with under-40s. For people or things: *T'es relou !*, *C'est relou*. Neutral: *pénible*, *agaçant*.

Pissed off / Furious

Literally: Verlan of *énervé*.

*Elle est trop vénère contre lui.*
She's really pissed at him.

💡 Informal verlan of *énervé*. *Je suis vénère* = I'm furious. Friends only; neutral: *Je suis énervé(e)* / *en colère*.

To freak out / be scared

Literally: From English *to flip*.

*Je flippe pour l'examen.*
I'm freaking out about the exam.

💡 Informal. *Ça fait flipper* = that's scary. *J'ai flippé* = I freaked out. Neutral: *avoir peur*, *paniquer*.

To be starving (slang)

Literally: To have the slab.

*J'ai la dalle, on mange ?*
I'm starving, shall we eat?

💡 Informal. Conjugate *avoir*: *J'ai la dalle !* Friends only; neutral: *J'ai très faim*.

To leave / clear off

Literally: To break oneself.

*Bon, je me casse, à demain !*
Right, I'm off, see you tomorrow!

💡 Informal. *Je me casse* = I'm off. *Casse-toi !* = Get lost! (rude). Neutral: *partir*, *s'en aller*. Don't confuse with *se casser la jambe* (break).

It's a nightmare / a hassle.

Literally: It's the galley.

*Trouver un appart à Paris, c'est la galère.*
Finding a flat in Paris is a nightmare.

💡 Informal, very common. Verb: *galérer* = to struggle: *J'ai galéré pour trouver un appart*. Neutral: *C'est compliqué / pénible*.

It's freezing!

Literally: It curdles!

*Ferme la fenêtre, ça caille !*
Close the window, it's freezing!

💡 Informal. Fixed form: *Ça caille !* — friends and family. Neutral: *Il fait très froid*.

To mess up / get it wrong

Literally: To plant oneself.

*Je me suis planté à l'exam.*
I messed up the exam.

💡 Informal. Also 'to crash' (car, computer). Reflexive: *Je me suis planté(e) à l'exam*. Neutral: *se tromper*.

Car (wheels)

*On prend ta bagnole ?*
Shall we take your car?

💡 Informal; also *la caisse*. Feminine: *ma bagnole*. Neutral: *la voiture*.

Clothes

*Elle dépense tout en fringues.*
She spends everything on clothes.

💡 Informal, always plural: *J'ai acheté des fringues*. Neutral: *les vêtements*.

A book

*Tu as fini ton bouquin ?*
Have you finished your book?

💡 Informal but harmless, fine with most people; *bouquiner* = to read. Neutral: *un livre*.

A party

Literally: Verlan of *fête*.

*Il y a une teuf chez Léa samedi.*
There's a party at Léa's on Saturday.

💡 Informal verlan of *fête*, youth. *Faire la teuf* = to party. Neutral: *une fête*, *une soirée*.

That's cool! / Stylish!

Literally: It's styled!

*Ta veste est trop stylée !*
Your jacket is so cool!

💡 Youth slang, friends only. Praises looks or an idea: *Ta veste est trop stylée !* Neutral: *C'est cool / C'est sympa*.

To have a bad cold

Literally: To have the death.

*J'ai chopé la crève.*
I caught a stinker of a cold.

💡 Informal. Conjugate *avoir*: *J'ai la crève*. Also *attraper la crève* = to catch your death of cold. Neutral: *J'ai un gros rhume*.

To be fed up to the back teeth

Literally: To have it up to the brim of the bowl.

*J'en ai ras le bol de ce boulot !*
I'm fed up with this job!

💡 Informal. Add *de*: *J'en ai ras le bol de ce boulot*. Also *ras-le-bol* as a noun. Image: the bowl is full to the brim. Polite: *J'en ai assez*.

To queue / wait in line

Literally: To make the tail.

*On a fait la queue pendant une heure.*
We queued for an hour.

💡 Neutral, everyday. *Faire la queue pour…* = to queue for. Careful: *queue* is also slang for penis, but this phrase is totally standard.

To greet with cheek kisses

Literally: To make the kiss.

*En France, on se fait la bise pour dire bonjour.*
In France, people greet each other with cheek kisses.

💡 Neutral; number of kisses varies by region (2 in Paris)! Conjugate + indirect pronoun: *On se fait la bise ?* *Je lui fais la bise*. Colleagues often shake hands instead.

To be ravenous / could eat a horse

Literally: To have a wolf's hunger.

*Après le sport, j'ai une faim de loup.*
After sport I'm ravenous.

💡 Neutral. Conjugate *avoir*: *J'ai une faim de loup !* Image: hungry as a wolf.

To suddenly feel exhausted

Literally: To have a bar blow.

*J'ai un gros coup de barre après le déjeuner.*
I hit a wall after lunch.

💡 Informal. Conjugate *avoir*: *J'ai un coup de barre* — classic after lunch. Neutral: *un coup de fatigue*.

To sleep like a log

Literally: To sleep like a dormouse.

*Les enfants ont dormi comme des loirs.*
The kids slept like logs.

💡 Neutral. *Un loir* = a dormouse, which hibernates for months. *J'ai dormi comme un loir*.

To rack one's brains / go to a lot of trouble

Literally: To break one's head.

*Ne te casse pas la tête, commande une pizza.*
Don't go to any trouble, order a pizza.

💡 Informal, everyday. Reflexive: *Je me suis cassé la tête sur ce problème*. Often negative as reassurance: *Ne te casse pas la tête !* = don't go to any trouble.

To have a mental blank

Literally: To have a memory hole.

*Désolé, j'ai un trou de mémoire, tu t'appelles comment ?*
Sorry, my mind's gone blank — what's your name?

💡 Neutral, fine at work. *J'ai eu un trou de mémoire* = my mind went blank. Image: a hole in your memory.

To give up (guessing)

Literally: To give one's tongue to the cat.

*Je ne trouve pas… je donne ma langue au chat !*
I can't get it… I give up!

💡 Neutral, playful; for riddles and guessing games. *Je donne ma langue au chat !* = I give up, tell me!

To have goosebumps

Literally: To have chicken flesh.

*Cette chanson me donne la chair de poule.*
This song gives me goosebumps.

💡 Neutral. Conjugate *avoir*: *J'ai la chair de poule*; *Ça me donne la chair de poule* = it gives me goosebumps. Image: skin like a plucked hen's.

To have a frog in one's throat

Literally: To have a cat in the throat.

*Pardon, j'ai un chat dans la gorge.*
Sorry, I've got a frog in my throat.

💡 Neutral. The French have cats, the English frogs. *J'ai un chat dans la gorge*.

To kill two birds with one stone

Literally: To make two hits with one stone.

*Je passe à la banque et à la poste : d'une pierre deux coups.*
I'll do the bank and the post office: two birds, one stone.

💡 Neutral, fine at work. Conjugate *faire*: *J'ai fait d'une pierre deux coups*. Image: one stone, two hits — no birds harmed.

To pitch in / lend a hand

Literally: To put one's hand in the dough.

*Tout le monde a mis la main à la pâte pour le déménagement.*
Everyone pitched in for the move.

💡 Neutral. Means joining in the actual work, not just watching: *Tout le monde doit mettre la main à la pâte*. Image: hands in the dough.

To be completely wrong

Literally: To put one's finger in one's eye.

*S'il pense que je vais payer, il se met le doigt dans l'œil !*
If he thinks I'm paying, he's sorely mistaken!

💡 Informal. Conjugate reflexively: *Tu te mets le doigt dans l'œil !* = you're kidding yourself. Stronger: *jusqu'au coude* (up to the elbow). Neutral: *se tromper complètement*.

To fall through (plans)

Literally: To fall in the water.

*Notre projet de vacances est tombé à l'eau.*
Our holiday plans fell through.

💡 Neutral. Conjugate with *être*: *Notre voyage est tombé à l'eau*. Subject is the plan, not the person.

To be in one's element

Literally: To be like a fish in water.

*Sur scène, elle est comme un poisson dans l'eau.*
On stage, she's in her element.

💡 Neutral, a compliment. Conjugate *être*: *Elle est comme un poisson dans l'eau ici*. Opposite: *comme un poisson hors de l'eau*.

Something's fishy / up.

Literally: There's an eel under the rock.

*Ils chuchotent depuis ce matin… il y a anguille sous roche.*
They've been whispering all morning… something's up.

💡 Neutral, a bit old-fashioned but well known. Fixed form: *Il y a anguille sous roche*. Image: an eel hiding under a rock.

To stump someone (with a tough question)

Literally: To put down a glue.

*Ah, tu me poses une colle, je ne sais pas.*
Ah, you've got me there, I don't know.

💡 Informal. Conjugate + indirect pronoun: *Tu me poses une colle !* = you've got me there. Reply when you don't know: *Ah, là, tu me poses une colle.*

To be too busy to step back and think

Literally: To have one's head in the handlebars.

*En ce moment, j'ai la tête dans le guidon au travail.*
Right now I'm totally snowed under at work.

💡 Informal; from cycling — head down over the handlebars, not seeing the road. *J'ai la tête dans le guidon en ce moment*. Common at work.

To be very generous

Literally: To have one's heart on one's hand.

*Ma grand-mère a le cœur sur la main.*
My grandmother is incredibly generous.

💡 Neutral, a compliment. Conjugate *avoir*: *Elle a le cœur sur la main*. Image: holding your heart out to give.

To be a scaredy-cat / chicken

Literally: To be a wet hen.

*Saute ! Ne sois pas une poule mouillée !*
Jump! Don't be such a chicken!

💡 Informal, teasing. Applies to men and women: *T'es une poule mouillée !* Neutral: *froussard(e)*, *peureux/peureuse*.

To worm information out of someone

Literally: To pull the worms out of someone's nose.

*Elle a fini par me tirer les vers du nez.*
She eventually got it out of me.

💡 Informal. Conjugate + indirect pronoun: *Elle m'a tiré les vers du nez*. Usually implies patient questioning.

To beat around the bush

Literally: To turn around the pot.

*Arrête de tourner autour du pot et dis-moi !*
Stop beating around the bush and tell me!

💡 Neutral. Often imperative: *Arrête de tourner autour du pot !* Opposite: *aller droit au but*.

cards.front: **Ne pas y aller par quatre chemins**
cards.back:
To get straight to the point / be blunt

Literally: To not go there by four paths.

*Je ne vais pas y aller par quatre chemins : c'est non.*
I'll get straight to the point: it's no.

💡 Neutral; always negative. Conjugate: *Je ne vais pas y aller par quatre chemins*. Often announces bad news. Image: no detours, one road straight there.

To give someone a telling-off

Literally: To pass someone a soap.

*Mon père m'a passé un savon.*
My dad gave me a real telling-off.

💡 Informal. Conjugate + indirect pronoun: *Mon père m'a passé un savon*, *Je me suis fait passer un savon* = I got told off. Neutral: *gronder*, *réprimander*.

To run off as fast as possible

Literally: To take one's legs to one's neck.

*En voyant le chien, il a pris ses jambes à son cou.*
When he saw the dog, he legged it.

💡 Neutral, humorous image: legs thrown around your neck. Conjugate + possessive: *Il a pris ses jambes à son cou*. Usually passé composé.

To be at the end of one's rope

Literally: To be at the end of the roll.

*Avec le bébé, je suis au bout du rouleau.*
With the baby, I'm at the end of my rope.

💡 Informal. Conjugate *être*: *Je suis au bout du rouleau*. Exhausted physically or mentally — fine to say at work. Image: the end of the roll.

To tighten one's belt

Literally: To tighten one's belt.

*Ce mois-ci, il faut se serrer la ceinture.*
This month we've got to tighten our belts.

💡 Neutral. Reflexive: *On doit se serrer la ceinture ce mois-ci*. Same image as English.

To throw money down the drain

Literally: To throw money out of the windows.

*Acheter ça ? C'est jeter l'argent par les fenêtres.*
Buy that? It's throwing money away.

💡 Neutral, usually critical. Conjugate: *Il jette l'argent par les fenêtres*. Image: throwing money out of windows.

To be rolling in money

Literally: To roll on gold.

*Ils ne roulent pas sur l'or, mais ils sont heureux.*
They're not rolling in it, but they're happy.

💡 Neutral; often in the negative: *On ne roule pas sur l'or* = we're not exactly rich. Image: rolling on gold.

cards.front: **Avoir les yeux plus gros que le ventre**
cards.back:
To have eyes bigger than one's stomach

Literally: To have eyes bigger than the belly.

*Trois desserts ? Tu as les yeux plus gros que le ventre.*
Three desserts? Your eyes are bigger than your stomach.

💡 Neutral, light-hearted — said about food or overambitious plans. Conjugate + possessive: *J'ai eu les yeux plus gros que le ventre*.

cards.front: **Ça ne casse pas trois pattes à un canard.**
cards.back:
It's nothing special / nothing to write home about.

Literally: It doesn't break three legs of a duck.

*Le film ? Ça ne casse pas trois pattes à un canard.*
The movie? Nothing to write home about.

💡 Informal, humorous; always negative. Spoken: *Ça casse pas trois pattes à un canard*. Image: a three-legged duck would be remarkable — this isn't.

To have a memory like a goldfish

Literally: To have a goldfish's memory.

*Rappelle-moi demain, j'ai une mémoire de poisson rouge.*
Remind me tomorrow, I've got a memory like a goldfish.

💡 Informal, self-deprecating. Conjugate *avoir*: *J'ai une mémoire de poisson rouge*. Same image as English.

To be stubborn as a mule

Literally: To be stubborn like a mule.

*Inutile d'insister, il est têtu comme une mule.*
No point insisting, he's stubborn as a mule.

💡 Neutral. Also *têtu comme un âne*. Agree: *Elle est têtue comme une mule*. Often affectionate criticism.

To be big-headed

Literally: To have the big head.

*Depuis sa promotion, il a pris la grosse tête.*
Since his promotion he's become big-headed.

💡 Informal, critical. Conjugate *avoir*: *Il a la grosse tête depuis sa promo*. Slangier: *avoir le melon*. Neutral: *être prétentieux*.

To turn a deaf ear

Literally: To make the deaf ear.

*Je lui demande de ranger, mais il fait la sourde oreille.*
I ask him to tidy up but he turns a deaf ear.

💡 Neutral. Conjugate *faire*: *Il fait la sourde oreille*. Means deliberately ignoring a request — not literal deafness.

To rest easy / sleep soundly

Literally: To sleep on both one's ears.

*Les portes sont fermées, tu peux dormir sur tes deux oreilles.*
The doors are locked, you can rest easy.

💡 Neutral; about having no worries. Often reassuring: *Tu peux dormir sur tes deux oreilles* = you can rest easy.

cards.front: **C'est la goutte d'eau qui fait déborder le vase.**
cards.back:
That's the last straw.

Literally: It's the drop of water that makes the vase overflow.

*Encore en retard ? C'est la goutte d'eau qui fait déborder le vase !*
Late again? That's the last straw!

💡 Neutral. Often just *C'est la goutte d'eau*. Image: the drop that makes the vase overflow — like English 'last straw'.

It's all over / We're done for.

Literally: The carrots are cooked.

*Il reste deux minutes, on perd 3-0 : les carottes sont cuites.*
Two minutes left, we're losing 3-0: it's all over.

💡 Informal, humorous; fixed form. Said when there's no hope left: *À 3-0 à la 85e minute, les carottes sont cuites.*

To make someone suspicious / tip someone off

Literally: To put the flea in the ear.

*Son sourire m'a mis la puce à l'oreille.*
His smile made me suspicious.

💡 Neutral. Subject is the clue, object the person: *Son sourire m'a mis la puce à l'oreille*. Image: a flea in your ear makes you alert.

To bet one's life on it

Literally: To put one's hand in the fire.

*C'est lui, j'en mettrais ma main au feu.*
It's him, I'd bet my life on it.

💡 Neutral. Usually *J'en mettrais ma main au feu* = I'd swear to it. Negative: *Je n'en mettrais pas ma main au feu* = I wouldn't swear to it.

To split the difference / meet halfway

Literally: To cut the pear in two.

*Tu veux 100, moi 60 : coupons la poire en deux.*
You want 100, I want 60: let's meet halfway.

💡 Neutral, fine at work and in negotiations. *On coupe la poire en deux ?* = Shall we meet in the middle?

To be a huge hit

Literally: To make a tobacco.

*Sa chanson a fait un tabac cet été.*
Her song was a huge hit this summer.

💡 Neutral, fine at work. Subject is the show/product/person: *Son film fait un tabac*. Youthier: *faire un carton*.

To have a green thumb

Literally: To have the green hand.

*Regarde ses tomates, elle a la main verte !*
Look at her tomatoes, she's got green fingers!

💡 Neutral, a compliment. Conjugate *avoir*: *Ma mère a la main verte*. Note: the hand, not the thumb.

To be bold / fearless

Literally: To not have cold eyes.

*Partir seule en Amazonie ? Elle n'a pas froid aux yeux !*
Going alone to the Amazon? She's got guts!

💡 Neutral, a compliment (sometimes 'cheeky'); always negative. *Il n'a pas froid aux yeux*.

To get turned down (romantically)

Literally: To take a rake.

*Je lui ai demandé son numéro, je me suis pris un râteau.*
I asked for her number and got shot down.

💡 Informal. Reflexive in passé composé: *Je me suis pris un râteau*. Similar: *se prendre une veste*. Neutral: *se faire rejeter* / *essuyer un refus*.

A cop / The cops

Literally: *Keuf* is verlan of *flic*.

*Attention, les keufs arrivent !*
Watch out, the cops are coming!

💡 Informal; *keuf* is verlan youth slang. *Flic* is widely used but avoid it with officers. *Un policier* is the neutral word; *les forces de l'ordre* is formal.

A liar / bullshitter

Literally: Short for *mythomane*.

*Arrête de mytho, personne ne te croit !*
Stop making stuff up, nobody believes you!

💡 Youth slang; verb *mytho* or *mythonner*. Short for *mythomane*. *Arrête de mytho !* = stop lying. Neutral: *un menteur / une menteuse*.

Bro

Literally: Verlan / diminutive of *frère*.

*Ça va, frérot ?*
How's it going, bro?

💡 Youth slang, between close friends. *Reuf* is verlan of *frère*; *frérot* is affectionate (also for actual brothers). Female: *ma reus* / *sœurette*.

Yo! / Hey!

*Wesh, bien ou quoi ?*
Yo, how's it going?

💡 Youth / street slang; from Algerian Arabic. Can sound try-hard if overused. Use only with friends who say it themselves; neutral: *Salut !*

Thanks!

Literally: Verlan of *merci*.

*Cimer pour le plan, frérot !*
Thanks for the tip, bro!

💡 Youth slang, playful; verlan of *merci*. Friends only — always *merci* with strangers. Also *Cimer, frère !*

It's a mess / chaos.

Literally: It's the brothel.

*Ta chambre, c'est le bordel !*
Your room is a total mess!

💡 Informal, mildly vulgar — avoid at work. Softer: *c'est le bazar*. *Quel bordel !* = what a mess! (*bordel* originally means brothel).

Better late than never.

Literally: Late is worth more than never.

*Tu as enfin appelé ! Mieux vaut tard que jamais.*
You finally called! Better late than never.

💡 Proverb, everyday — said to someone arriving late or finally doing something. Neutral, fine anywhere.

Time will tell.

Literally: Who will live will see.

*Est-ce que ça va marcher ? Qui vivra verra.*
Will it work? Time will tell.

💡 Proverb, everyday, neutral. Said when the outcome is uncertain. Shorter casual equivalent: *On verra*.

Bad (or good) things come in threes.

Literally: Never two without three.

*Deuxième fois que je rate le bus… jamais deux sans trois !*
Second time I've missed the bus… things come in threes!

💡 Proverb, used jokingly after something happens twice — e.g. a second breakage or a second win. Neutral.

Great minds think alike.

Literally: Great minds meet.

*— J'allais commander la même chose ! — Les grands esprits se rencontrent.*
— I was going to order the same thing! — Great minds think alike.

💡 Saying, playful — said when you and someone have the same idea at the same time. Neutral, fine at work.
